item.title: MDMA (Molly) for PTSD: Hope, Hype, and Hard Evidence
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

MDMA (Molly) for PTSD: Hope, Hype, and Hard Evidence

Ecstasy is MDMA. Can this empathogen help people with PTSD?

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • A review/meta-analysis found MDMA-assisted therapy improves PTSD symptoms, but evidence certainty is low.
  • Positive trials establish lasting remission, adequate safety, and effectiveness in ordinary clinical practice.
  • VA and independent investigators are testing MDMA with different therapies, populations, and dosing.
  • FDA approval for now is uncertain.

Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a potentially disabling disorder affecting approximately 8% of U.S. adults over their lifetime. Military veterans have even greater PTSD risks; as high as 21% of Gulf War veterans experience PTSD. I reported that MDMA-assisted psychotherapy may improve PTSD symptoms. in adults. But how certain are we? That’s the central finding of an October 2026 Neuropsychopharmacology review by current Stanford Ph.D. student Brooke Sevchik and her former colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania. They rated overall evidence as low certainty.

The investigators analyzed six randomized trials involving 286 participants. They found that MDMA-assisted therapy produced greater short-term improvement than control treatment. The pooled analysis found remission from PTSD was more than twice as likely with MDMA-assisted therapy. Impressive.

But questions remain about the overall quality of clinical trials due to blinding—subjects aren’t supposed to know if they received the test drug or placebo, but with drugs like MDMA, they usually do know—and remission at the end of trials. All six trials shared one sponsor, the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS). While it bravely kept the field alive, the trials used closely related MAPS-associated psychotherapy protocols. So, these were not six independent replications.

Sevchik’s analysis found no statistically significant improvement in depression (often accompanying PTSD), although a separate meta-analysis reported broader benefits. The investigators also created an open database that can be updated as new evidence appears. Good. Conclusions should change when evidence changes.

Why Did the FDA Initially Say No to MDMA?

Two Phase 3 trials reported favorable outcomes, but the FDA declined approval in August 2024. Concerns around those trials included inadequate blinding, potential expectancy bias, aspects of psychotherapy delivery, and questions about safety and the reliability of efficacy estimates. Positive results were not enough to meet FDA standards.

But a Presidential Executive Order gave another chance to MDMA to resolve questions that remain about lasting recovery and also trial quality, particularly blinding and influence on improvement ratings. Participants receiving MDMA recognize its unmistakable psychoactive effects, while those receiving placebo may guess they received a sugar pill. The April 2026 presidential initiative accelerating psychedelic research adds momentum, but not evidence. Executive orders cannot substitute for randomized trials.

Resilient Pharmaceuticals, formerly Lykos, reportedly resubmitted its application to the FDA in August 2026. A resubmission is another chance to convince the FDA to approve the drug.

Why Might MDMA Help People With PTSD?

People with PTSD may experience intrusive memories of traumatic events years later. Sometimes the danger feels immediate, as though they are back at the original trauma site. Patients may avoid reminders of trauma, difficult conversations, and sometimes treatment itself.

article continues after advertisement

MDMA increases serotonin signaling and affects dopamine, norepinephrine, and brain circuits involved in fear, emotional processing, and social reward. It may reduce fear and make patients more receptive to psychotherapy.

Although oxytocin is commonly associated with childbirth and breastfeeding, it is also a neuropeptide involved in social behavior, attachment, and reward learning. Animal studies suggest that MDMA can reopen a critical period for social reward learning through an oxytocin-dependent mechanism. A 2025 meta-analysis also found temporary increases in blood oxytocin after MDMA administration. Whether these findings explain improvement in PTSD remains uncertain.

There is an interesting parallel with GLP-1 medications used for obesity and diabetes. These medications also influence brain reward circuitry and are being investigated as addiction treatments. Their mechanisms differ substantially from MDMA, but both illustrate how drugs can influence motivation, reward, and behavior.

MDMA vs. GLP-1s
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

MDMA may temporarily change the conditions under which emotional and social learning occur. But does it produce lasting changes in traumatic memories, or only temporary changes in emotional experience? Clinical trials must answer that question.

PTSD's established treatments—including prolonged exposure therapy, cognitive therapy, and EMDR—already help many patients. We need to determine what MDMA adds to these treatments.

The VA Is Asking Better Questions

The VA announced a randomized trial involving approximately 80 veterans with PTSD and alcohol use disorder. Participants will receive psychotherapy along with MDMA or the use of low-dose MDMA as an active placebo. Other studies may clarify optimal dosing, treatment frequency, and the required psychotherapy. Questions about these things remain unanswered.

article continues after advertisement

Veterans frequently have complicated clinical presentations. Co-occurring alcohol problems cannot be ignored, so including this diagnosis was a good idea.

The VA's clinical guidance appropriately describes MDMA as experimental. Its official review emphasizes limitations within existing research, particularly for veterans.

The VA is funding the answers. MDMA in this context is a drug under serious consideration.

Independent Trials May Change Everything

Emory University is studying MDMA combined with prolonged exposure therapy, an established PTSD treatment. The planned randomized trial will enroll 95 participants and examine symptoms, fear-related brain responses, and durability. Does MDMA enhance an already-effective treatment? Final results are expected by January 2030.

Other independent investigators are studying alternative approaches. For example, a Sheba Medical Center trial in Israel plans to compare group and individual MDMA-assisted therapy following the October 7 attacks and the subsequent development of PTSD. Both groups will receive MDMA, so there is no placebo group. This study may answer an important question: Can treatment be delivered more efficiently?

Who Pays for Treatment?

An October Fierce Pharma commentary raised another problem: Psychedelic treatments are expensive, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale. And MDMA-assisted therapy is no ordinary psychiatric office prescription.

Research protocols involve prolonged drug sessions, preparation, follow-up psychotherapy, trained clinicians, and weeks of care.

So, who pays for all those expenses? Who trains therapists? And what happens in rural communities? Will insurers cover treatment for veterans living in the sticks? An effective treatment unavailable to most patients is hardly a public-health triumph.

Other companies are developing psychedelic and MDMA-like treatments, including Transcend Therapeutics. Competition may improve treatment options — or produce more expensive options.

article continues after advertisement

“Ecstasy” Is Still Ecstasy

Meanwhile, MDMA continues its other life as a popular black-market and recreational drug. Users seek energy, euphoria, intimacy, and intensified sensory events.

Street ecstasy may contain uncertain amounts of MDMA, ketamine, or other drugs. MDMA by itself can cause severe side effects, including hyperthermia, hyponatremia, seizures, cardiovascular complications, and serotonin toxicity.

Clinical supervision reduces some risks but cannot eliminate adverse reactions. Strict drug controls are also necessary to prevent diversion.

What is still needed are independent replication, better masking and measurement of expectations, systematic safety monitoring, longer controlled follow-up, and direct comparisons with established PTSD treatments.

We also need outcomes beyond symptom scores. Can patients return to work, maintain relationships, sleep well enough, and function better, months or years after PTSD treatment?

The October Neuropsychopharmacology review provides a useful starting point for where we stand with MDMA for PTSD: short-term benefit, low certainty, and important unanswered questions.

Veterans deserve innovation. So do civilians with disabling PTSD. But they also deserve treatments that work, remain effective, and don't create new problems.

MDMA deserves serious research. Enthusiasm is welcome.

Evidence is better.

item.title: Evaluating the Impact of Environmental Art
item.description:
Environment

Evaluating the Impact of Environmental Art

Bob Turner of Colgate University discusses measuring impact of environmental art

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Environmental art has a larger impact on those who do not already have strongly pro-environment attitudes.
  • Visuals are more likely to create emotional effects and educate viewers about environmental issues.
  • Measurement should be based on psychological and behavioral theories.
Source: Elena Mozhvilo / Unsplash

Humans use art to focus their creative imagination to interpret or reflect reality, convey thoughts and emotions, or provoke new ideas and feelings in others. Art can alter environmental norms, which consist of beliefs, attitudes, and behavior that foster a caring and responsible relationship to the environment in four principal ways: (1) by fostering empathy and stimulating moral imagination, (2) by promoting narrative transportation and increasing cognitive engagement, (3) by providing new symbols for identity construction and stimulating processes of value alignment, and (4) by communicating in public spaces and affording experiential learning within the pedagogical milieu of the arts.

How can creative community leaders, policymakers, and artists utilize art to influence environmental norms in targeted ways? To answer this question, I spoke to Bob Turner, an emeritus Professor of Economics and Environmental Studies at Colgate University. His research has focused on the intersection of art and environmental awareness. I asked Bob what I think are important questions that policymakers and community leaders should be asking.

JP: How do we measure the effectiveness of art that is intended to influence environmental norms and behavior?

BT: It’s hard. In fact, I think it’s impossible to answer the question in general. But it’s possible, though difficult, to answer a narrower question: How do we measure the effectiveness of a particular piece of art on a particular group of people in a particular place over a particular span of time? The particulars of how to measure the impact of exposure to art on attitudes, perceived norms, and intended behaviors will depend on the particular setting: who is being observed, the type of exposure, the length of exposure time, and whether it’s a short-run or long-run effect that one wants to measure. But there are two key issues, regardless of the particulars: measurement should be grounded in behavioral theory, and controlling for confounding factors (other factors that may be correlated with exposure to art) is crucial but difficult.

JP: What are some aspects of the behavioral theory you mention?

BT: Several psychological theories could be the basis for measurement: for example, the Theory of Planned Behavior, Value-Belief-Norm Theory, and norm-activation models. There are also sociological explanations of behavior. Many of these theories have common elements that can inform researchers’ inquiries: people have (no doubt differing) fundamental values, beliefs, and worldviews as well as behavior-specific attitudes; there are relevant norms, both personal and social and both environment-specific and general; there are factors influencing the activation and moderation of values, goals, and norms; and there are constraints that affect the efficacy of all these things on behavioral change. In line with those behavioral theories, researchers have used responses to questionnaires and survey questions to measure attitudes, perceived norms, and behavior.

article continues after advertisement

JP: And how do you control for confounding factors?

BT: That is indeed crucial but difficult: How do we know that any changes we observe after exposure to environmental art are due to the environmental art and not due to other factors that may have also changed along with the exposure to environmental art or due to differing characteristics of those who were exposed versus those who weren’t? To make things even more difficult, these confounding factors are often not observable or measurable themselves. To deal with confounding factors, especially those that are unobservable, one can make comparisons, like a treatment group versus a control group in a medical trial.

An especially promising technique, when it’s available, is to do a before-and-after comparison: measure attitudes, perceived norms, and behavior before and after exposure to environmental art and see what’s changed. This controls for unobserved characteristics of the people being exposed to environmental images, though it’s still possible that other factors influencing the response changed during the exposure.

Or, even better, do what is sometimes called difference-in-difference estimation: compare the amount by which one group changed before and after exposure to the amount by which another group changed. This controls for unobserved characteristics of people as well as things that changed during the time of exposure, if those things happened to all the people being observed.

JP: What does your research suggest about the impact of visual communication aimed at changing environmental attitudes, beliefs, and intended behavior?

BT: My findings are mixed, but I’ve found evidence that short exposure to visual images and text often has a measurable impact, especially on people who don’t already have strongly pro-environmental attitudes and beliefs. It’s suggestive that longer exposure would have even larger effects.

JP: Does visual communication have a special role, versus strictly textual communication?

BT: There’s a literature suggesting reasons why visual imagery might have a larger impact. My own research suggests that, in general, there isn’t much difference in impact on environmental attitudes, beliefs, or intended behaviors between the images and videos I have used and text, though in some cases combining the two seems most effective. But when I looked specifically at people who aren’t already strongly pro-environment, there’s stronger evidence that visual imagery has a larger impact.

JP: What are the arguments that visual communication has a larger impact?

BT: My own research provides only weak evidence in support of these arguments, but visuals are more likely to create an emotional effect in addition to educating viewers about environmental issues. Text is more likely to work solely through cognitive interest and reasoned choice, which arguably has a lower impact without the emotional effect associated with visual communication. Visual communication may be especially effective in terms of creating motivation through the emotional affect I mentioned earlier.

article continues after advertisement

Videos, in particular, can utilize cinematic literary devices such as narratives, metaphors, and comedy that may stir the types of affective responses that arguably lead to behavioral changes. Videos that integrate environmental activism can also visualize the issue in creative ways that may resonate with viewers, thereby inspiring them to take action.

item.title: Who Decides What Mental Health Care Insurance Covers?
item.description:
Law and Crime

Who Decides What Mental Health Care Insurance Covers?

Insurers’ profits versus patients’ needs and access to services.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Patients with mental health concerns often require health insurance to cover medically necessary services.
  • Insurance companies should prioritize patient needs when determining whether insurance covers services.
  • Patients and clinicians may raise questions when insurance coverage is denied.
  • Patients and clinicians should understand their rights to appeal insurance denial decisions.

In a series of court processes dating back to 2014, judges have examined how health insurance companies should balance their responsibilities to people seeking mental health care against their own financial interests (Wit v. United Behavioral Health, 2023, 2026). Insurance companies have financial incentives to limit reimbursements for services and maximize profits for shareholders. However, when administering certain employer-sponsored health plans,1 insurers have fiduciary duties requiring them to prioritize the interests of plan participants and beneficiaries over their own financial interests (cf., Employee Retirement Income Security Act, 1974). These obligations are similar, although not identical to the fiduciary responsibilities of psychologists and other mental health professionals (MHPs) to their clients (ACA, 2014; APA, 2017; NASW, 2021).

Ordinarily, access to mental health treatment should be based on patient needs and wishes (Olejarczyk & Young, 2024). Health insurance is intended to facilitate access to covered services, including psychotherapy, inpatient care, outpatient treatment, and other mental health and addictions services. But what happens when an insurer's financial interests conflict with its responsibilities to the people it insures?

What Are Generally Accepted Standards of Care?

Generally accepted standards of care refer to clinical principles and evidence-based treatment guidelines broadly recognized by mental health professionals as appropriate for assessing and treating patients (Wit v. United Behavioral Health, 2023). There is no singular set of standards of care that apply to all contexts of practice or all treatment decisions. Standards may vary for particular mental health concerns, diagnoses, and client situations. Across various types of treatment decisions, however, accepted standards of care should typically:

  • address underlying conditions rather than simply stabilize immediate crises;
  • consider co-occurring disorders;
  • provide treatment at a safe and effective level of care; and
  • tailor treatment duration to individual needs (Wit v. United Behavioral Health, 2023).

Importantly, clinically appropriate treatment may include services that maintain functioning or prevent deterioration, even when patients are not experiencing an acute crisis (e.g., suicide plans). In Wit v. United Behavioral Health (2023), courts explored whether the insurer's internal guidelines were more restrictive than these standards and whether financial considerations improperly influenced its coverage policies. However, treatment consistent with generally accepted standards of care is not necessarily covered under every insurance plan. To determine what is or what is not covered by a particular insurance plan, one needs to look at the terms of the plan, as well as relevant healthcare insurance laws.

What Are Possible Reasons for Denying Coverage?

Insurance companies may provide a variety of reasons for denying insurance coverage. For example, insurers may refuse continued hospitalization because a patient's immediate crisis has stabilized, deny further psychotherapy because symptoms are not improving, or require patients to try less intensive services before authorizing the treatment their clinicians recommend. Insurance companies may determine that a particular type of treatment is not medically necessary; they may require prior authorization for particular services; or they may have restrictions involving providers or facilities where services may be obtained (U.S. Department of Labor, 2016).

Other denials may involve arbitrary limits on treatment duration, failure to consider co-occurring disorders, overly restrictive definitions of medical necessity, or insufficient access to qualified in-network providers. Although some restrictions are permitted under insurance contracts and applicable law, others may be inconsistent with generally accepted standards of care or federal mental health parity requirements (described below).

Treatment decisions and insurance coverage determinations should consider each patient’s individual clinical needs and circumstances, rather than rely on arbitrary or overly restrictive criteria (e.g., limiting inpatient treatment for patients with suicidal thoughts to a predetermined number of days).

How Do Mental Health Parity Laws Apply?

The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act is intended to protect patients against discriminatory insurance practices. Under these federal laws, covered health plans generally cannot impose more restrictive financial requirements or treatment limitations on mental health and substance use disorder benefits than on comparable physical health care, medical treatments, and surgical benefits. These protections extend to certain practices involving prior authorization, medical necessity determinations, and other restrictions on access to care. Accordingly, an insurance company's coverage guidelines may raise legal concerns not only when they conflict with generally accepted standards of care, but also when mental health benefits are administered more restrictively than comparable medical benefits (U.S. Department of Labor, 2016).

What Can Patients and Clinicians Do When Coverage Is Denied?

When insurance coverage is denied for particular services, patients and their clinicians may consider what steps to take to appeal the decision (U.S. Department of Labor, n.d.). Patients can request written explanations of denied benefits (U.S. Department of Labor, n.d.), obtain the insurance company’s guidelines used to make coverage decisions, and appeal denials through their insurance plans. If an internal appeal is unsuccessful, they may be entitled to independent external review. Note that a denial is not automatically unlawful simply because a treating clinician disagrees with it. Clinical appropriateness, relevant laws, and the terms of the insurance contract must also be considered.

Challenging insurance company decisions can be challenging, particularly for clients who are already experiencing anxiety, depression, distress, or other mental health concerns. They may need assistance from patient advocates, clinicians, or family members.

Clinicians can help clients by accurately documenting their clinical needs, explaining why recommended services are medically necessary, and providing research evidence based on generally accepted standards of care. When interacting with insurance companies, clinicians should use conflict management strategies and skills, including active listening, option generation, clarification, and problem-solving (Barsky, 2017).

When denials create risks to patient safety or continuity of care, clinicians should also explore expedited appeals and appropriate interim treatment arrangements. Patients may seek assistance from their employers (human resources), state insurance regulators, the U.S. Department of Labor, or legal counsel when they believe an insurer has violated applicable laws or improperly restricted access to care.

Note that denial of coverage may be technically consistent with an insurer's internal policy yet still raise questions about whether that policy itself was developed appropriately. As in the Wit case, it may be necessary for one or more patients to hire attorneys to challenge insurance policies that violate relevant laws.

Although insurance can facilitate access to needed mental health services, patients, their clinicians, and other support systems often must advocate for coverage when insurers initially deny treatment. Ultimately, the responsibility for ensuring access to appropriate care should not rest solely on those seeking treatment, but also on the insurers entrusted with administering their benefits fairly and responsibly.

Footnote:

  1. This article focuses on employer-sponsored health plans. Laws and processes related to Medicare and Medicaid may differ.

item.title: Why "Dancing With the Stars" Is So Popular
item.description:
Parasocial Relationships

Why "Dancing With the Stars" Is So Popular

A psychotherapist explains why "Dancing With the Stars" appeals to so many.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • "Dancing With the Stars" offers viewers a weekly dose of inspiration and joy.
  • Watching others step outside their comfort zone can inspire us to grow, too.
  • Inclusive casting highlights what's possible when people lead with resilience, optimism, and hope.

It's Thursday morning, and my client is in a better mood than usual.

"Was there something you did differently this week that's contributed to feeling like your 'emotions felt more consistent,' as you mentioned?"

"It might sound strange," she begins, "but I'm watching Dancing With the Stars for the first time. It's so touching—I cried twice during last night's episode!"

I nod knowingly, because I did, too.

Coincidentally, this was also my first time watching the show. I had watched So You Think You Can Dance back in the day and am no stranger to reality TV, but Dancing With the Stars was never of interest to me until this year. And apparently I'm not alone: Its current 35th season, which began last month, has garnered 6.67 million viewers across ABC and Disney+, a 24% jump from the previous year. It's also the show's biggest audience since 2020.

So, what is it about rookies trying ballroom dancing that's so entertaining and appealing?

1. The courage to be a beginner

There is something deeply moving about watching accomplished, well-known people have the bravery to try something new in front of millions of viewers. After all, most of us like to avoid situations where we might look foolish. It can be tempting to stick with hobbies we're good at, skip karaoke night because we aren't a singer, and stay within our comfort zones. On Dancing With the Stars, we watch celebrities do the exact opposite: They stumble through rehearsals, struggle to pick up choreography, cry in frustration, and then walk onto a live stage anyway.

Psychologists have a name for the warm, uplifted feeling we get from witnessing this kind of courage. Research by Sara Algoe and Jonathan Haidt, published in The Journal of Positive Psychology, found that witnessing others' goodness and talent evokes emotions like elevation and admiration, which are associated with feeling inspired and motivated to become better people ourselves.

This is the main reason I've fallen in love with the show myself. This season, I've been especially impressed by Ezra Frech, a man who was born without most of his left leg and missing fingers on his left hand. With a prosthetic leg since he was 11 months old, Frech received two gold medals during the 2024 Summer Paralympics in Paris—one for the men's 100-meter race and one for the men's high jump. Seeing his resilience and positive attitude firsthand on the show is a source of inspiration, not just entertainment. And hey, if he and other celebrities can learn a quickstep in a week, maybe the idea of taking on a new challenge myself seems a little less daunting.

2. A feel-good refuge in turbulent times

Between political division, global conflict, economic uncertainty, and an endless scroll of headlines, many of my clients describe feeling chronically on edge, as though they're bracing for the next bad thing.

Against that backdrop, Dancing With the Stars is two hours of pure, uncomplicated joy. Nobody is being humiliated. Nobody is plotting a backstabbing alliance. Even when they provide constructive criticism, the judges share feedback from a place of care. The contestants cheer each other on, and the worst thing that happens in a given week is that someone goes home with a hug and a tearful thank-you speech. When the world feels heavy, it makes perfect sense that we'd reach for something wholesome, warm, and hopeful.

Just as our bodies need rest after physical exertion, our nervous systems need moments of lightness to recover from sustained stress. For me, the show has become an unexpected, accessible way to practice self-care.

3. Representation and resilience

Over the years, Dancing With the Stars has made room for a wide range of identities and abilities. It has featured drag queens and same-sex partnerships alongside deaf contestants and people living with chronic illnesses like multiple sclerosis. They're there to compete, and sometimes they're the most compelling dancers of the season. Watching someone who can't hear feel the beat through vibrations in the floor challenges our assumptions about what bodies can do and who gets to take up space on a stage. For viewers who share their experiences, it can be a powerful moment of feeling seen. For everyone else, it's a reminder of how much strength exists in the people around us.

There's psychological research to suggest this kind of visibility matters. The parasocial contact hypothesis, developed by Edward Schiappa and colleagues, proposes that positive exposure to members of a group through media can reduce prejudice in much the same way that real-life contact does.

4. Broadening our range

Perhaps my favourite part of this season is watching people joyfully expand their sense of who they are.

Take Tyler Cameron, a contestant from The Bachelorette and former football player. Week after week, we've watched him fully commit to learning dance routines and genuinely enjoying the art and sport of dance. There's something wonderful about seeing a man who may have grown up in a world of tough masculinity discover that he can also be expressive, playful, and graceful—and that those qualities don't cancel each other out.

Or there's the male, heterosexual dance coach from Season 31 who was partnered with Shangela, a well-known drag queen from Ru Paul's Drag Race. He treats her exactly as he would any of his heterosexual female partners: with respect, warmth, and physical affection so that she looks and feels her best. (And yes, I'm also watching Season 31 now because the whole live, one-episode-a-week thing is simply too little Dancing With the Stars for me right now.)

Sociologist Eric Anderson's theory of inclusive masculinity suggests that as cultural attitudes become more accepting, men feel freer to express emotional openness, physical tenderness, and interests once considered "unmasculine" without fear of losing "status." In many ways, the ballroom is a living example of this shift. These are men who are broadening our definitions of masculinity without any shame attached to it.

Takeaway

Taken together, these four threads point to why we might cry over a Pasa Doble: It's not just for the entertainment, but for the reminder that perhaps there's more kindness, encouragement, and bravery in the world than we sometimes realize.

item.title: Why Feeling Like We Belong Matters So Much
item.description:
Relationships

Why Feeling Like We Belong Matters So Much

What a movie can teach us about community, connection, and finding home.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Belonging is a fundamental psychological need that extends beyond our closest relationships.
  • Feeling at home often has less to do with a place than with the people and experiences that connect us to it.

It’s the most wonderful time of the year: The Hallmark Countdown to Christmas. Families are at the center of so many of the stories we watch, whether we recognize it or not. As a family scientist, I'm interested in how these stories reflect what research tells us about family relationships—and where popular portrayals differ from what we know.

In this blog series, I'll use familiar stories from popular culture to explore the science of family life, examining the relationships, experiences, and everyday interactions that shape how we connect with one another.

Lyndsy Fonseca (as Avery), Robert Buckley (as Matt)
Source: Hallmark Media

"Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story"

Hallmark Christmas movies have a fairly predictable formula: Someone arrives in a new place (or returns to an old one), discovers an unexpected connection, and begins reconsidering what matters most in life. Usually, romance plays a central role. But sometimes the more interesting love story isn't between two people; it's between a person and a community. That's what makes Hallmark's Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story an interesting opportunity to consider the psychology of belonging.

This movie features Avery Clark, an ambitious freelance reporter who returns to Chicago for Christmas. Accustomed to moving often for work, Avery knows little about football or the city. When she begins profiling Darlene Donnelly, a devoted Chicago Bears fan preparing to attend her 500th game, Avery encounters a community connected through shared traditions, collective memories, and a sense of identity.

Belonging Is More Than Having Relationships

Psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary argued that people have a strong motivation to form and maintain lasting, positive interpersonal relationships. Importantly, belonging isn't simply about being surrounded by people. We can have numerous social interactions and still feel disconnected. Meaningful belonging involves feeling accepted, valued, and connected to others.

These connections can be particularly important when our lives are changing. Moving, changing careers, entering a new relationship, or experiencing other transitions can disrupt established social networks and leave us searching for new ways to connect.

For someone like Avery, whose career involves frequent change, the appeal of a stable community may be about more than finding romance. It may represent the possibility of becoming part of a shared story.

Why Sports Fans Feel Like Family

Social identity theory suggests that our identities are shaped partly by the social groups to which we belong. We don't define ourselves solely as individuals. We also understand ourselves as members of families, communities, professions, and other groups. For devoted sports fans, team identification can become a meaningful part of that social identity. For example, Wann and colleagues found that a sense of belonging helped explain the relationship between sports fandom and perceived meaning in life. In other words, supporting a team may provide something that extends far beyond entertainment.

article continues after advertisement

Fans share experiences, celebrate victories, endure disappointments, and develop connections with people they might otherwise never meet.

Traditions Connect Us Across Generations

One of the most compelling elements of Holiday Touchdown is Darlene's extraordinary history as a Bears fan. Attending 500 games represents far more than an impressive attendance record. Those games are connected to relationships, memories, and important moments across her life.

Family scholars recognize that rituals and traditions can serve important functions in maintaining family identity and connection. Whether families gather for holiday meals, celebrate birthdays in particular ways, or watch football together every Sunday, these repeated experiences provide continuity.

Research on family rituals suggests that these practices can support family cohesion and provide a sense of stability and identity. A family that gathers to watch football may spend surprisingly little time discussing the game. Instead, the gathering becomes an opportunity to share meals, tell stories, reconnect, and create memories.

This isn't the first time Hallmark has used football to illustrate the importance of family traditions. In last year's Holiday Touchdown: A Bills Love Story, I explored how shared rituals can strengthen family identity and create connections across generations. This year's Bears-themed movie builds on that idea by highlighting something equally important: how traditions can connect us not only to our families but also to a broader community.

Finding Home Isn't Always About Finding a Place

We often think of home as a physical location, but home can represent something more complex. It may be the place where people know our stories and recognize our traditions. Sometimes, home isn't a place at all but the experience of being connected. This is an important distinction because people don't necessarily need to remain geographically close to experience belonging. Families maintain traditions across distances, friends develop communities through shared interests, and people establish meaningful connections in new places.

article continues after advertisement

Belonging also doesn’t require everyone to share the same interests. Avery doesn't need to become a lifelong football fanatic to appreciate what the Bears mean to Darlene and her family. Sometimes, connection begins with curiosity about why something matters so much to someone else.

Hallmark vs. Psychology

Hallmark Christmas movies may not be known for their realism, but that doesn't mean they don't get some things right. Throughout this series, I'll end each post with a reality check. Sometimes the movies will get the science right, sometimes they'll take a few creative liberties, and sometimes the answer will fall somewhere in between.

Hallmark says: Sometimes finding where you belong means finding the right people, traditions, and community to call home.

Psychology says: There's real science behind this one! Our sense of belonging isn't limited to romantic relationships or even our immediate families. Shared experiences, meaningful traditions, and connections across generations can strengthen our social identities and help us feel part of something larger than ourselves.

The verdict: Hallmark gets this one right. The most meaningful love story isn't always romantic; sometimes, it's about finding your people.

item.title: Do You Heal From the Inside Out or the Outside In?
item.description:
Therapy

Do You Heal From the Inside Out or the Outside In?

When in doubt about how to heal, go for the happy middle.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Some people and professionals believe that we can't move forward until we resolve our past.
  • Others believe that by changing our present through new thoughts and skills, we change our lens on the past.
  • A middle ground is learning the lessons of the past, while learning new coping skills in the present.
Source: geralt/pixabay

At the risk of oversimplifying, there are two types of people and two types of therapy: those who believe change comes from the inside out and those who believe it comes from the outside in. Here are the characteristics and limitations of each:

Inside Out

This is the stuff of classic psychodynamic approaches, which focus heavily on unraveling the past and gaining insight. This perspective also appeals to those who feel their emotional wounds are holding them back and that they can’t move forward until they resolve past wounds or trauma. Essentially, the paradigm is that I need to feel better to do better.

Limitations: While effective and understandable, this approach has a few risks. One obvious risk is that your life is essentially on pause until the past is resolved. Another is that the process can be challenging: Delving into the past can become a deep rabbit hole for some, who discover ever more layers of wounds and trauma as they dig deeper.

Finally, on the practical side, there is time and money—evacuating can often be a months- or years-long project. Even if you feel you are making progress, both the treatment and the wounds continue to shape your everyday life.

Outside In

I hear clients who have had extensive therapy say, “I’m sick of talking about my past; let’s not go down that childhood road again.” In contrast to the inside focus of feeling better to do better, outside people believe in doing better to feel better. This lends itself to cognitive-behavioral approaches, which focus on the present, resolve current problems, and build skills, using homework to change dysfunctional thinking and behaviors. Often, as you change your present, you also view your past through a different lens.

Limitations: The downside of this approach is that it can become a psychological forced march: Yes, learning new skills is great, but the lessons insiders draw from the past are often lost. Wounds that don’t require a deep dive into the past often benefit from some attention—recent or old grief comes to mind. Unless wounds are acknowledged and addressed, even briefly, they can become an undertow that undermines real progress.

Finding That Happy Middle

So, is there a win-win compromise between these seemingly different factions — a Goldilocks "just-right" middle? I think so. One part of healing requires having a first-aid plan in place. For most of us, our past wounds are triggered by specific situations in the present—for example, a critical comment from your boss or a sudden change of plans that rattles you. Your rational brain goes offline; your emotional brain takes over. Knowing what your triggers are can help you handle them better—anticipate them, arrange support if needed, and stay centered when they flare up so you don't feel overwhelmed.

But you can also do some work outside of these vulnerable times: Engage in brief therapy to address specific aspects of your past or learn new self-regulation skills.

The middle ground is about moving forward and looking ahead to a bright future without being hindered by the past.

item.title: Why We Can Never Just "Relax"
item.description:
ADHD

Why We Can Never Just "Relax"

In a world of hustle and self-optimising, doing nothing is a radical act.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • From childhood, we’re pushed to decide what we’ll become and rarely allowed to simply exist.
  • Many women with ADHD struggle to sit at peace, but even a few quiet seconds can bring insight.

I can never relax. I think there have only been a handful of moments in my entire existence on this earth when I have truly just sat in Being. I have a vivid memory of looking out the school window as a child, sitting in the classroom and watching a dog randomly roam around the playground. I had a peculiar envy for this carefree creature. Not only did it not have to sit in a stuffy classroom all day learning times tables, but it could just 'exist'. There was no constant pressure to do something, achieve something, amount to something.

It starts young, when adults ask little children, “What do you want to be when you grow up?” This harmless question always makes me sad. Can’t they just be allowed to exist as children? The time will come soon enough when they’ll be bombarded with exams and deadlines and nerve-jangling moments when they have to decide which life path to go down. I remember my sister asking my nephew, “What do you want to be when you grow up?” He didn’t have an answer. “I don’t know,” he said, looking confused. “Well,” my sister told him, “you’d better think of something. We all have to work.” She meant it as a joke, but it made my heart sink. We all have to do something. We all have to work. The curse of being human is not being allowed to just exist. We can never be like that dog in the playground.

In this era of late-stage capitalism, hustle culture and self-optimisation, maybe the most radical move of all is to say no and decide to do nothing. Imagine that: a radical act of defiance in 2026.

Let me tell you about one of the rare moments when I just existed on this planet, without my head buzzing onto the next task, the next objective, the next shiny object. I had just read a book called Effortless Being, which guided me through how to sit in absolute stillness. For the first time in years, my mind emptied of all thoughts. I imagine it must be like cleaning the filter of your dishwasher after years of neglect. For the first time in year my mind was…blank. It’s a hard state to get into, as it seems to go against every human instinct. Most of our minds chatter away at us 24/7 like constant background radio static. When I finally achieved this elusive stillness, it felt like a clearing in a forest. I felt like I was above the clouds for a moment, away from all the noise of life.

And of course, my brain buzzed again with a thought. But this one felt different. It was a clear direction to email a university professor about a PhD project investigating women with ADHD. I emailed her, and I got it. And that’s how you’re reading this article today. I am currently researching the lives and careers of women entrepreneurs with ADHD. I know this all sounds a tad “woo-woo”, but I think we’re all allowed one woo-woo story to peddle. That is mine.

As an ADHD woman myself, I know I’m not alone in my general inability to sit at peace and enjoy existing. But if you do get a moment, even a few seconds, to quiet your mind and just exist like that dog in the playground, you might be amazed at what insights come to you. Your mind is a truly fascinating machine. Go ahead, try it.

item.title: Is It Heterophobia or Is Gen Z Redefining Intimacy?
item.description:
Relationships

Is It Heterophobia or Is Gen Z Redefining Intimacy?

Why younger generations are questioning sex, romance, and the risks of connection.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Young adults are navigating competing fears of rejection, sexual harm, and social judgment.
  • Changing gender expectations may be reshaping how people approach romantic and sexual intimacy.
  • Attachment theory can offer insight into the tension between wanting connection and fearing vulnerability.
  • IFS helps distinguish intentional singlehood from protective avoidance of intimacy and vulnerability.

A newly married male client described a recurring complaint from his wife: He wasn't assertive enough. Yet he struggled to understand how to express sexual desire without appearing aggressive. Having grown up hearing about sexual harassment, assault, and the importance of consent, he worried that initiating intimacy might make his wife uncomfortable.

Another client, a woman approaching 30, had never had a boyfriend or experienced sexual intercourse. She described herself as sex-positive but privately felt like a fraud. How could she embrace sexual freedom while feeling so uncertain about her own sexuality?

These experiences reflect something I am increasingly encountering in my clinical practice: Young adults who desire intimacy but approach dating and sex with considerable hesitation. Their concerns suggest a growing divide in how men and women understand attraction, vulnerability, and emotional safety.

The New Anxiety Around Dating

For Gen Z, dating unfolds within a culture of heightened awareness about consent, gender inequality, and interpersonal harm. These conversations are necessary, but they coexist with uncertainty about how to initiate romantic connections.

Some young women describe fearing that potential partners will reveal misogynistic attitudes associated with the online “manosphere,” disregard boundaries, or perpetrate sexual violence. Meanwhile, some young men express fears of rejection, public embarrassment, or being perceived as “cringe,” threatening, or overly aggressive when expressing romantic or sexual interest. These competing anxieties can create uncertainty around dating, with men struggling to distinguish healthy assertiveness from unwanted pursuit and women navigating the tension between a desire for intimacy and concerns about emotional and physical safety.

These fears are not equivalent. Women's concerns about sexual harm are grounded in documented experiences of harassment and violence. Men's uncertainty about changing expectations represents a different, though psychologically meaningful, challenge.

Pew Research Center (Brown, 2020) found that 47 percent of American adults believed dating had become harder over the previous decade. Additionally, 65 percent believed increased attention to sexual harassment and assault had made it harder for men to know how to behave on dates.

The challenge is not that consent education has gone too far. Rather, we have become more sophisticated in identifying harmful behavior without always developing equally sophisticated models of healthy desire, mutual initiation, and relational communication.

Are Younger Generations Having Less Sex?

Research suggests that sexual behavior among young people has been changing for years. Twenge and colleagues (2017) documented declines in sexual activity among American adults, particularly younger cohorts.

However, declining sexual activity does not necessarily indicate declining interest in intimacy. Some young adults are delaying relationships, prioritizing education, reconsidering traditional gender roles, or finding fulfillment outside romantic partnerships.

Digital culture also changes how relationships develop. Rosenfeld and colleagues (2019) found that online dating had overtaken introductions through friends as the most common way heterosexual couples met.

For some, digital dating expands possibilities. For others, it transforms connection into a process of evaluation, comparison, and perceived disposability.

Generation Alpha, whose oldest members are only entering adolescence, is still too young for reliable conclusions about adult sexual trends. Nevertheless, the attitudes toward relationships they encounter online may influence their developing expectations.

Gen Z is rethinking dating, sex, and intimacy. They are exploring fears, shifting gender roles, attachment, and emotional safety, which shapes the desire for connection and the choice to remain single.
Source: cottonbro studios / Pixels

Heterophobia and the Growing Gender Divide

The term heterophobia has appeared in some cultural conversations about growing distrust, frustration, or avoidance between heterosexual men and women. Historically, however, heterophobia has referred to fear or hostility toward heterosexuality. Its newer usage should not be confused with an established clinical diagnosis or a scientifically demonstrated generational phenomenon.

What deserves attention is the possibility that heterosexual relationships are becoming associated with conflict rather than connection.

Online narratives sometimes portray men as inherently dangerous or emotionally unavailable and women as excessively demanding or impossible to satisfy. These generalizations can reinforce defensiveness and distrust before two people even meet.

These tensions are also present within communities of color, where dating and intimacy are shaped by the intersection of cultural values, racialized experiences, gender expectations, and broader social pressures. Across diverse cultural backgrounds, individuals may navigate competing expectations about masculinity, femininity, sexuality, and relationships while confronting stereotypes, discrimination, and intergenerational beliefs about intimacy. A culturally humble approach recognizes that these experiences are not universal and that race, culture, gender, sexuality, and personal history influence how individuals understand attraction, vulnerability, safety, and connection.

Attachment Theory: When Connection Feels Unsafe

Attachment theory provides another perspective.

Bowlby (1988) described how early relational experiences can shape expectations about emotional availability, trust, and security. Adult attachment research further demonstrates how anxiety and avoidance can influence romantic relationships (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016).

Someone with attachment anxiety may desire closeness while fearing rejection or abandonment. Someone with avoidant tendencies may minimize romantic needs to protect against vulnerability.

Contemporary dating culture can intensify these patterns. Ghosting, ambiguous relationships, social comparison, and inconsistent communication may activate fears of inadequacy or rejection.

For some, avoiding dating becomes a protective strategy rather than an absence of desire.

Friendship as an Alternative to Romance

Not every decision to remain single reflects fear.

Some young adults are intentionally investing in friendships, chosen families, and community relationships, rather than organizing their lives around romantic partnership.

Research by Holt-Lunstad and colleagues (2010) demonstrates the importance of social relationships for health and well-being.

Expanding our understanding of intimacy beyond romantic and sexual relationships can be psychologically healthy. Platonic relationships provide opportunities for emotional vulnerability, reciprocity, affection, and belonging.

The clinical question is whether someone is freely choosing these relationships or using them exclusively to avoid the vulnerability of romantic connection they actually desire.

An Internal Family Systems Perspective

Internal Family Systems (IFS) offers a compassionate framework for exploring these conflicting desires.

Schwartz and Sweezy (2019) describe how protective parts attempt to prevent emotional pain, often through avoidance, control, or self-criticism.

A young man may have a part that desires sexual connection and another that fears being perceived as aggressive. A young woman may have a part that values sexual exploration alongside another that fears judgment, vulnerability, or harm.

Rather than labeling these contradictions as dysfunction, therapy can explore what each protective part fears might happen.

The goal is not to persuade someone to date or become sexually active. It is to develop enough internal safety, self-awareness, and agency to make choices that reflect their authentic desires and values.

Moving Toward Connection Without Fear

Perhaps younger generations are not rejecting intimacy as much as questioning the expectations surrounding it.

Their hesitation invites us to reconsider how we teach healthy sexuality. Consent matters, but so do communication, mutual desire, relational repair, and the ability to tolerate vulnerability.

We need models of intimacy in which assertiveness does not require aggression, boundaries do not eliminate spontaneity, and sexual experience is not a measure of personal worth.

The question may not be why young people are afraid of dating, but whether we are giving them the relational tools to feel safe enough to connect.

item.title: Why We Can Feel Invisible Even When Surrounded by People
item.description:
Friends

Why We Can Feel Invisible Even When Surrounded by People

A conversation with John Miles on friendship and the science of mattering.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • Make your care visible. Tell people what you appreciate about them and why they matter to you.
  • Vulnerability and authenticity help us feel known not just socially connected.
  • Make room for reciprocity. Healthy relationships leave room for both offering and receiving care.
  • Success can make us visible to the world without making us feel valued.

I recently spoke with author John Miles, whose book The Mattering Effect: Creating a Life of Meaning and Worth was released on October 6. We discussed the science of mattering, the role of reciprocity in relationships, and why so many of us can appear successful while feeling invisible.

Dr. Marisa Franco: In your book, you talk about how a traumatic brain injury you experienced as a child shaped your understanding of mattering. Can you share more about that experience?

John Miles: When I was a child, I experienced a traumatic brain injury after being pushed through a basement window. I woke up in intensive care, surrounded by machines, with a tube in my head. I don’t remember much about the incident itself, but I remember realizing that my life was going to be different. I didn’t know how dramatically, but I knew I had changed.

The injury affected my eyesight, caused chronic headaches and sensory and auditory processing issues, and left me with a significant speech impediment. I struggled in school, and other kids teased me.

My speech therapist was someone I hated visiting because I had to walk in front of the entire classroom to get to her office, with everyone staring at me. But she also helped me discover something important. She essentially taught me what we now call a growth mindset: I could accept my circumstances as fixed, or I could work to overcome my limiting beliefs and become the author of my own life.

That mindset shaped the next decade of my life. Then, in high school, I had a career counseling session with a teacher I deeply admired. I had been accepted to Duke, Michigan, the Naval Academy, and several other schools. I was trying to figure out what came next. During that conversation, she told me that it didn’t matter where I went to college because I would never do anything meaningful with my life. I would never amount to anything, she said, and would always live in mediocrity.

If my brain injury hadn’t changed the trajectory of my life, that conversation did.

Years of working to rebuild my sense of self and overcome challenges seemed to evaporate in a 20-minute discussion. I would spend the next 25 years living in what I now call the mattering gap—trying to prove that I was enough.

MF: That’s horrible, and I’m sorry you experienced it. Your story illustrates so poignantly how much other people influence our sense of mattering. That teacher communicated that you didn’t matter. What can we do differently in our friendships and relationships to help people feel that they do?

JM: I think attachment science offers a useful way to understand this. When people feel unsafe or insignificant, they can develop anxious or avoidant attachment patterns. I believe a deep, prolonged sense of insignificance can contribute to both.

article continues after advertisement

For me, it manifested as avoidance. I repeatedly received the signal that my real self wasn’t seen or needed, so I started withdrawing from the world and presenting a different version of myself. Over time, that became a slow disappearance of self. I felt invisible.

I think of anxious attachment as overpaying the mattering tax: continually working to earn the reassurance that you matter. With avoidant attachment, it’s as if you eventually go bankrupt and shut the account altogether.

Researcher Isaac Prilleltensky describes mattering as having two sides: giving value and receiving value. We need to know that we matter to others, and we need to feel that we contribute something meaningful. But we tend to overemphasize how we provide value to others, and our culture rewards us for doing.

In our relationships, we need to reinforce how much people matter to us—not just in broad statements, but in concrete, specific ways. The more detailed we can be about what someone means to us, the more likely they are to feel it.

MF: You also write about how we sometimes struggle to receive care, even when other people are trying to show us that we matter. Why does that happen, and how can we get better at receiving care?

JM: I think we minimize our emotional needs to create physical or psychological distance from other people. Having experienced avoidant attachment for so many years, I’ve relied heavily on self-sufficiency. Letting people in has been difficult because of the trust issues I developed through my experiences.

One way we begin to change this is by initiating the first cue of care. When we start offering care to others, we can create opportunities for them to respond with care in return.

MF: It sounds like you’re pointing to how busy and overwhelmed we all are. We may not even realize when we’re failing to show care or reciprocate the care someone else gives us.

article continues after advertisement

JM: Exactly. When I first started trying to understand my own experience, I described myself as numb, burned out, broken, and indifferent to the world.

But as I looked more closely, I realized what I was really experiencing: I was highly visible to the outside world, yet I felt completely invisible within it.

I think that’s what so many people are experiencing today. That realization led me to study self-worth, mattering, belonging, and self-determination theory. I wanted to understand why we can be surrounded by people and still feel unseen.

MF: I think many people can relate to having friends in name but not necessarily feeling connected to them. One thing I appreciated about your book is your emphasis on authenticity and vulnerability. We have to express ourselves and let people see who we really are if we want to feel connected—even when we already have people to spend time with.

JM: Vulnerability has been difficult for me, particularly in my friendships with other men. I’ve had very few relationships with men in which I felt I could be completely myself.

One of those friendships was especially important to me. My friend died by suicide about a decade ago. He was someone I could call at 2 in the morning or tell my deepest secrets to without worrying that he would use them against me or make me feel small.

After he died, I found myself wondering what more I could have done for him. He had been there for me so consistently, but he hadn’t told any of us about the financial difficulties that were weighing on him. When we eventually learned what was happening, several of us could easily have helped him financially.

I spent the Saturday before he died with him. We went out, danced, listened to music, and had a great time. He spent Sunday with two other close friends. Looking back, I sometimes wonder whether he knew what he was going to do.

I share this because it made me think about why someone who gave so much care to others might not ask for that same care in return.

article continues after advertisement

When you don’t feel that you matter, it can be incredibly difficult to believe that other people would want to help you. Even when care is available, you may not be able to recognize it or ask for it.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: How to Negotiate With Your Inner Critic
item.description:
Self-Esteem

How to Negotiate With Your Inner Critic

Personal Perspective: Your inner critic means well, but still needs managing.

Posted October 19, 2026

Key points
  • In internal family systems therapy, your inner critic is called a protector.
  • Even if they are loud, harsh, and negative, they are genuinely trying to help.
  • But they do need managing at times, using a calm, collaborative approach.
Source: Mohamed Hasan/Pixabay

Because I have a new book out, I am doing lots of work to promote it, like writing blog posts, magazine articles and columns, being interviewed by various journalists and appearing on, to date, three podcasts. I have mostly enjoyed these things, even though some of them (writing) are much more in my comfort zone than others (podcasts).

But I recently noticed my inner critic getting very loud and uncomfortably forceful. This part of me is, of course, critical. But he (I don't like calling parts "it," as it seems a bit demeaning to me) is also highly perfectionistic, pointing out any little mistake I have made and urging me to do better next time.

On the most recent podcast, I/my critic felt I could have done much better at three specific points in the hour-long chat. To be clear, I was very happy with at least 90% of my answers. The hosts were kind and thoughtful. Overall, it was a very enjoyable experience. But guess what my mind kept spinning back to for the rest of that day? Yep, those three points I "messed up," as my critic so helpfully reminded me.

My Inner Dialogue: A Report

Honestly, it left me feeling both surprised and depressed: surprised because I have done so much work on this well-meaning but often clumsy part of me, and he is so much quieter than he used to be, and depressed because, well, berating yourself for hours is a proven way to lower your mood and keep it in the doldrums.

As an internal family systems (IFS) therapist, I speak to my parts on an ongoing, hour-by-hour basis, so I decided to have a chat with my critic. It went something like this...

Me: Woah, Critic, this is all a bit much. I hear you and get that you're trying to help – I think by pointing out my mistakes so I do better next time. But it's not helping. You're stressing me out and, frankly, making me feel awful.

Critic: But you did flub those lines – and you could do so much better.

Me: I know, and that wasn't ideal. But I nailed 90% of it and, honestly, no-one cares about those tiny mistakes as much as me or you. So listen, I totally get you are trying to help. And I do appreciate you for all the hard work you do trying to keep me safe. But it's too much, please take a break and let me learn from these mistakes, in my own way.

Critic: OK, I'll try to ease off a bit. I just think you could be awesome if you pushed a bit harder.

Me: I know, but honestly I don't have to be awesome, just good enough. All this pressure makes me very much not-awesome, because I get stressed and inarticulate, leading to the flubbing. Thanks for trying to give me a bit more space though, I really appreciate it.

A Message From My Self

Towards the end of this dialogue, another voice came in – and it was loud! This new voice said: "I don't need to be perfect, or awesome. I just want to be authentically, messily myself." And I love this, because it's exactly how and who I want to be. Where did this powerful, affirming message come from? In IFS therapy, we would see these wise, helpful thoughts as emanating from Self – the prefrontal cortex-based, loving, compassionate inner resource we all possess.

article continues after advertisement

And this message from my Self has really stayed with me, because it's the opposite of the perfectionistic idea that I must be perfect at all times, never make a mistake, or be seen as anything less than excellent. Authentically, messily myself means I'm OK being perfect or imperfect, succeeding or failing, being the most knowledgeable and articulate podcast guest ever, or flubbing some lines. I'm still more than good enough: messy, human, and lovable just as I am.

If any of this resonates with you, please use it as a rough guide when negotiating with your inner critic. In IFS, we call this part a protector. They mean well, even if that's hard to see sometimes. They are usually trying to motivate you ("Work harder! Be better!") or protect you by criticising you for something internally, so you avoid being criticised, shamed, or rejected externally. And the former is usually way less painful than the latter.

So, as I am always telling my clients, we never want to get angry or hostile with our critic, however frustrating they may be. Negotiating with them in this calm, collaborative manner is the most effective way to help them ease off a bit, give you a break, and let you do your thing, however imperfect and messy that may be.
